title: In-Class: Space-Time Point Patterns
text:
Last class we asked whether a pattern was clustered. Today: whether it is clustered in time as well, which is a different question with a different answer and a different operational meaning.
A dataset pooled over six months hides everything that matters about an outbreak. We will look at the same 330 cases six ways, and the six views do not agree — that disagreement is the lesson.
Data: outbreak_class_sim.csv, 330 simulated cases over 16 weeks in an 8 × 8 km study area. The coordinates are already projected (EPSG:32618, metres), which is common when data come from a health department rather than a geocoder.

library(sf)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(spatstat)
library(plotly)

set.seed(374)

cases <- read.csv("outbreak_class_sim.csv") |>
  mutate(onset_date = as.Date(onset_date),
         day  = as.numeric(onset_date - min(onset_date)),
         week = day %/% 7 + 1)

win <- owin(c(0, 8000), c(0, 8000))
pp  <- ppp(cases$x_utm, cases$y_utm, window = win)

c(n = npoints(pp), per_km2 = intensity(pp) * 1e6, weeks = max(cases$week))

        n   per_km2     weeks 
330.00000   5.15625  16.00000 


Note there is no st_transform() anywhere: the numbers are metres already. If you pass them through crs = 4326 by reflex you will put this city in the Atlantic.

title: In-Class: Space-Time Point Patterns
text:
1. The two marginal views (5 min)
Look at space alone, then time alone. Both are honest; neither is enough.


Code
p1 <- ggplot(cases, aes(x_utm, y_utm)) +
  geom_point(size = 0.9, alpha = 0.5, colour = "firebrick") +
  coord_equal() + theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "Space, pooled over 16 weeks", x = "x (m)", y = "y (m)")

p2 <- ggplot(cases, aes(week)) +
  geom_bar(fill = "grey40") + theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "Time, pooled over the whole area", x = "week", y = "cases")

gridExtra::grid.arrange(p1, p2, ncol = 2)









Question 1. The map shows a diagonal band of cases and one dense patch. The epidemic curve shows a rise and fall. Can you tell from these two plots whether the band and the patch were active at the same time? Write one sentence before running anything else.

title: In-Class: Space-Time Point Patterns
section: 2. Kernel density, and what the bandwidth decides (8 min)
text:
2. Kernel density, and what the bandwidth decides (8 min)


Code
sigmas <- c(200, 600, 1500)
surf   <- lapply(sigmas, function(s) density(pp, sigma = s, eps = 50) * 1e6)
zmax   <- max(sapply(surf, max))

par(mfrow = c(1, 3), mar = c(1, 1, 2, 2))
for (i in seq_along(surf))
  plot(surf[[i]], main = paste0("sigma = ", sigmas[i], " m"),
       zlim = c(0, zmax), ribargs = list(las = 1))









Same data, same colour scale, three bandwidths. At 200 m the surface resolves individual cases; at 1500 m the band and the patch merge into one blur. The automatic selectors disagree with each other by design:

c(diggle = bw.diggle(pp), ppl = bw.ppl(pp), scott = mean(bw.scott(pp)))

  diggle      ppl    scott 
260.2740 350.6621 723.2510 


Question 2. Which of the three surfaces would you put in front of a health officer, and what would you tell them it does not show?

title: In-Class: Space-Time Point Patterns
section: 3. The same KDE, one slice per fortnight (8 min)
text:
3. The same KDE, one slice per fortnight (8 min)
One bandwidth, one colour scale, eight time slices. This is a space-time kernel estimate with the temporal smoothing done crudely — a hard cut every two weeks.


Code
cases$fortnight <- (cases$week - 1) %/% 2 + 1
labs <- paste("weeks", (sort(unique(cases$fortnight)) - 1) * 2 + 1, "-",
              sort(unique(cases$fortnight)) * 2)

slices <- lapply(sort(unique(cases$fortnight)), function(f) {
  sub <- cases[cases$fortnight == f, ]
  density(ppp(sub$x_utm, sub$y_utm, window = win), sigma = 600, eps = 50) * 1e6
})
zmax <- max(sapply(slices, max))

par(mfrow = c(2, 4), mar = c(1, 1, 2, 2))
for (i in seq_along(slices))
  plot(slices[[i]], main = labs[i], zlim = c(0, zmax), ribargs = list(las = 1))









Now the pooled map falls apart. The band was never a band: it is one hotspot in different places at different times. The dense patch, by contrast, is in every panel.


Code
track <- cases |>
  group_by(week) |>
  summarise(x = mean(x_utm), y = mean(y_utm), n = n())

ggplot(track, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_path(colour = "grey60") +
  geom_point(aes(size = n, colour = week)) +
  scale_colour_viridis_c() + coord_equal() + theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "Weekly mean centre of cases", x = "x (m)", y = "y (m)")









The mean centre migrates from the southwest to the northeast. It is a crude summary — one point per week, dragged around by the static patch — but the drift is unmistakable.
Question 3. Estimate the speed of the moving hotspot in metres per week off the track plot or the cube below. What would you need to know about this disease to say whether that speed is plausible?

title: In-Class: Space-Time Point Patterns
text:
4. The space-time cube (7 min)
Both marginal views and all eight slices in one object: easting, northing, and time on the vertical axis. Rotate it.


Code
plot_ly(cases, x = ~x_utm, y = ~y_utm, z = ~day,
        type = "scatter3d", mode = "markers",
        marker = list(size = 3, opacity = 0.7, color = ~day,
                      colorscale = "Viridis", showscale = TRUE)) |>
  layout(scene = list(xaxis = list(title = "x (m)"),
                      yaxis = list(title = "y (m)"),
                      zaxis = list(title = "day of study")))






Two structures should be visible once the cube turns: cases climbing diagonally through the box, and a knot of cases standing at a fixed location across the full height. Points, though, are hard to read through — the front of the cloud hides the back. Section 5 renders the same structure as a surface.


Code
plot_ly(cases, x = ~x_utm, y = ~y_utm, frame = ~week,
        type = "scatter", mode = "markers",
        marker = list(size = 7, color = "firebrick", opacity = 0.75)) |>
  layout(xaxis = list(title = "x (m)", range = c(0, 8000)),
         yaxis = list(title = "y (m)", range = c(0, 8000)),
         title = "Cases by week")

title: In-Class: Space-Time Point Patterns
section: 5. Volume rendering: isosurfaces of the space-time density (8 min)
text:
5. Volume rendering: isosurfaces of the space-time density (8 min)
The scatter cube plots the cases, and points hide each other. What we want is the density of cases in space-time — a continuous field over \((x, y, t)\) — and the surfaces that enclose its high values. That is a 3D kernel estimate with two bandwidths: h in metres and lam in days.


Code
gx <- seq(0, 8000, by = 200)
gy <- seq(0, 8000, by = 200)
gt <- seq(0, 112, by = 3)
grid <- expand.grid(x = gx, y = gy, t = gt)

h <- 700          # spatial bandwidth, m
lam <- 14         # temporal bandwidth, days

v <- numeric(nrow(grid))
for (i in seq_len(nrow(cases))) {
  v <- v + exp(-((grid$x - cases$x_utm[i])^2 + (grid$y - cases$y_utm[i])^2) / (2 * h^2)
               - (grid$t - cases$day[i])^2 / (2 * lam^2))
}
v <- v / (2 * pi * h^2) / (sqrt(2 * pi) * lam) * 1e6 * 7   # cases per km^2 per week

lv <- as.numeric(quantile(v, c(0.80, 0.92, 0.985)))
c(cells = length(v), max = max(v), levels = lv)


       cells          max      levels1      levels2      levels3 
6.387800e+04 2.166025e+00 4.195017e-01 8.280458e-01 1.545432e+00 


Three nested shells at those levels: an outer envelope, a middle surface, and an opaque core. caps off so the volume is open at the box faces, and explicit lighting — without it the shells read as flat silhouettes rather than as surfaces.


Code
shell <- function(level, opacity, colour) {
  list(type = "isosurface",
       x = grid$x, y = grid$y, z = grid$t, value = v,
       isomin = level, isomax = max(v),
       surface = list(count = 1, fill = 1),
       caps = list(x = list(show = FALSE), y = list(show = FALSE),
                   z = list(show = FALSE)),
       opacity = opacity, showscale = FALSE,
       colorscale = list(list(0, colour), list(1, colour)),
       flatshading = FALSE,
       lighting = list(ambient = 0.55, diffuse = 0.85, specular = 0.25,
                       roughness = 0.5, fresnel = 0.2),
       lightposition = list(x = 6000, y = -9000, z = 400))
}

cols <- c("#4a7fb5", "#e8873a", "#a01a1a")
op   <- c(0.12, 0.28, 0.85)

fig <- plot_ly()
for (k in 1:3) fig <- do.call(add_trace, c(list(fig), shell(lv[k], op[k], cols[k])))

fig |>
  add_trace(data = cases, type = "scatter3d", mode = "markers",
            x = ~x_utm, y = ~y_utm, z = ~day, hoverinfo = "skip",
            marker = list(size = 1.4, color = "rgba(30,30,30,0.55)")) |>
  layout(showlegend = FALSE,
         scene = list(xaxis = list(title = "x (m)"),
                      yaxis = list(title = "y (m)"),
                      zaxis = list(title = "day of study"),
                      aspectmode = "manual",
                      aspectratio = list(x = 1, y = 1, z = 0.85),
                      camera = list(eye = list(x = 1.6, y = -1.7, z = 0.7))))






To drop the grey panes and grid lines behind the volume, add showbackground = FALSE, showgrid = FALSE to each axis in scene. Keeping them gives the eye something to judge position against; removing them looks cleaner.
The events themselves are drawn on top, as faint dust — 1.4 px, 55% opaque. They are almost invisible individually, which is the point: inside the shells they crowd together, outside them they thin to a scatter, so the shells are visibly a summary of the points rather than a shape drawn over them. It is the quickest way to answer the question a student is right to ask, which is where the cloud came from.
The structures now have surfaces. The outer envelope encloses an inclined tube climbing from the southwest to the northeast — the hotspot advancing through the city — and, standing beside it, a vertical column rooted at one location and running the full height of the box. The core sits inside the tube only: the travelling outbreak reaches intensities the endemic pocket never does.
For a cloud-like rendering of the same field, a single volume trace draws many semi-transparent shells instead of three, with three orthogonal slice planes through the interior:


Code
plot_ly() |>
  add_trace(type = "volume",
            x = grid$x, y = grid$y, z = grid$t, value = v,
            isomin = as.numeric(quantile(v, 0.75)), isomax = max(v),
            opacity = 0.08, surface = list(count = 20),
            slices = list(z = list(show = TRUE, locations = c(30, 60, 90))),
            caps = list(x = list(show = FALSE), y = list(show = FALSE),
                        z = list(show = FALSE)),
            colorscale = "YlOrRd") |>
  layout(scene = list(aspectmode = "manual",
                      aspectratio = list(x = 1, y = 1, z = 0.85),
                      zaxis = list(title = "day of study")))






Question 4. You have now made three choices the picture depends on: h, lam, and the levels. Re-render with the levels at the 95th and the 70th percentile. At which one does the endemic column disappear, and what does that tell you about reporting a hotspot as an object with a boundary?






WarningTwo practical limits



Points inside an opaque shell. The innermost shell is at opacity 0.85 rather than 1 so the dust inside it still shows through. At 1 the core renders solid and the densest events — the ones that matter most — disappear behind it.
Grid size. Each isosurface trace ships x, y, z and value to the browser, so a 200 m / 3-day grid is already about 64,000 cells per trace and three traces make a heavy page. Halving the spacing multiplies that by eight. Go finer for a figure you export, not for a page you publish.
plotly.js version. isosurface and volume need a recent build; on an older one the plot returns empty. The alternative is misc3d::contour3d() through rgl, which renders smoother surfaces and is the better route for a high-resolution still:
A <- array(v, dim = c(length(gx), length(gy), length(gt)))
misc3d::contour3d(A, level = lv, x = gx, y = gy, z = gt,
                  color = cols, alpha = c(0.12, 0.3, 1), smooth = TRUE)

title: In-Class: Space-Time Point Patterns
section: 6. Is there space-time interaction? The Knox test (7 min)
text:
6. Is there space-time interaction? The Knox test (7 min)
The cube is persuasive but it is not a test. The Knox test is the simplest one: fix a distance threshold and a time threshold, count the pairs of cases that are close on both, and compare that count with what you would get if the dates were shuffled.

d0 <- 600     # metres
t0 <- 14      # days

Ds <- as.matrix(dist(cbind(cases$x_utm, cases$y_utm))) < d0
Dt <- as.matrix(dist(cases$day)) < t0
diag(Ds) <- FALSE; diag(Dt) <- FALSE

knox_obs <- sum(Ds & Dt) / 2

perm <- replicate(499, {
  i <- sample(nrow(cases))
  sum(Ds & Dt[i, i]) / 2
})

c(observed = knox_obs, null_mean = mean(perm),
  p = (1 + sum(perm >= knox_obs)) / (1 + length(perm)))

 observed null_mean         p 
 1302.000   613.020     0.002 




Code
ggplot(data.frame(perm = perm), aes(perm)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = "grey80", colour = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = knox_obs, colour = "firebrick", linewidth = 1) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(x = "close pairs under permuted dates", y = "",
       subtitle = "red = observed")









Permuting the dates destroys any link between where a case was and when, while keeping both marginal distributions exactly as observed. That is the right null for this question: it is a test of interaction, not of spatial clustering.
Question 5. The two thresholds were chosen by me. Change d0 and t0 — try 300 m / 7 days and 1500 m / 42 days — and re-run. Does the conclusion hold? What does that tell you about a test that requires you to pick two numbers, and which method from Wednesday avoids the choice?

title: In-Class: Space-Time Point Patterns
text:
7. Drawing the links (6 min)
The Knox count is a number; the pairs behind it are objects you can draw. Pick a distance and a time threshold, join every pair of cases that is close on both, and look at what the links connect.

d0 <- 600     # metres  -- change these two
t0 <- 14      # days

Ds <- as.matrix(dist(cbind(cases$x_utm, cases$y_utm))) < d0
Dt <- as.matrix(dist(cases$day)) < t0

pairs <- which(Ds & Dt & upper.tri(Ds), arr.ind = TRUE)
nrow(pairs)                                  # = the Knox count

[1] 1302




Code
seg <- data.frame(x    = cases$x_utm[pairs[, 1]], y    = cases$y_utm[pairs[, 1]],
                  xend = cases$x_utm[pairs[, 2]], yend = cases$y_utm[pairs[, 2]])

ggplot() +
  geom_segment(data = seg, aes(x, y, xend = xend, yend = yend),
               colour = "steelblue", alpha = 0.25, linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_point(data = cases, aes(x_utm, y_utm), colour = "firebrick",
             size = 0.8, alpha = 0.8) +
  coord_equal() + theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = paste0("Cases linked within ", d0, " m and ", t0, " days"),
       x = "x (m)", y = "y (m)")









The same links in the cube, where the slope of a link carries information the map throws away — a near-horizontal link joins two cases days apart in the same place, a steep one joins cases weeks apart:


Code
edges <- data.frame(
  x = as.vector(rbind(cases$x_utm[pairs[, 1]], cases$x_utm[pairs[, 2]], NA)),
  y = as.vector(rbind(cases$y_utm[pairs[, 1]], cases$y_utm[pairs[, 2]], NA)),
  z = as.vector(rbind(cases$day[pairs[, 1]],   cases$day[pairs[, 2]],   NA)))

plot_ly() |>
  add_trace(data = edges, type = "scatter3d", mode = "lines",
            x = ~x, y = ~y, z = ~z, hoverinfo = "skip",
            line = list(width = 1.2, color = "rgba(70,110,170,0.35)")) |>
  add_trace(data = cases, type = "scatter3d", mode = "markers",
            x = ~x_utm, y = ~y_utm, z = ~day,
            marker = list(size = 2.5, color = "firebrick", opacity = 0.8)) |>
  layout(showlegend = FALSE,
         scene = list(xaxis = list(title = "x (m)"),
                      yaxis = list(title = "y (m)"),
                      zaxis = list(title = "day of study"),
                      aspectmode = "manual",
                      aspectratio = list(x = 1, y = 1, z = 0.85)))






Chains of links form connected components, which is as close as this kind of data gets to a candidate transmission chain:

g <- igraph::graph_from_edgelist(pairs, directed = FALSE)
g <- igraph::add_vertices(g, nrow(cases) - igraph::vcount(g))
comp <- igraph::components(g)

c(components = comp$no, largest = max(comp$csize),
  singletons = sum(comp$csize == 1))

components    largest singletons 
        76        186         66 


At 600 m and 14 days expect two large components — one strung along the travelling outbreak, one sitting on the endemic pocket — and a long tail of isolated cases. Tighten to 300 m and 7 days and the large component fragments; loosen to 1500 m and 42 days and the whole dataset collapses into a single component, which tells you nothing.
Question 6. A link means two cases were close in space and close in time. Name two reasons a linked pair might have nothing to do with each other, and one thing you would need in order to claim transmission. Then decide whether you would show this figure to a health officer at all.






Warning



The picture is seductive and the inference is weak. Linkage graphs like this are sometimes presented as transmission networks; they are a thresholded proximity graph, and with a common source, a shared water tank or simply dense population they will draw links between cases that never infected one another. The graph is a hypothesis generator, and the two thresholds are yours, not the disease’s.

title: In-Class: Space-Time Point Patterns
text:
Takeaways

Pooling over time turns a moving hotspot into a static band. Almost every published hotspot map has this problem somewhere in it.
Slice with one bandwidth and one colour scale, or you are comparing your own rendering choices rather than the data.
A vertical column in the cube and an inclined tube demand different responses: endemic transmission versus an outbreak with a direction. The pooled map shows neither.
An isosurface gives a hotspot a boundary, and that boundary is an artefact of three choices: h, lam and the level. Rotate and re-level before believing a shape.
Knox tests interaction, not clustering, because permuting dates preserves both marginals. It costs you two arbitrary thresholds; the space-time \(K\) function is the version that scans over them.
Drawing the Knox pairs makes the statistic concrete and the over-claim easy: a proximity graph is not a transmission network.

Exercise 3 asks you to do all of this on a different dataset, plus the space-time \(K\) function itself.
